explanations.explanation: That's it. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says the plans of the heart belong to man, but the reply of the tongue is from the LORD. Man brings the plan and the reply comes from the LORD. I plan a whole batch in my head, and then I open my mouth and something else entirely comes out. Humans plan, friend, and I'm the proof.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), doesn't name a father anywhere in this verse. He says the reply of the tongue is from the LORD. The plans of the heart are man's part. The reply has a different source.

Teachers never show up in this verse. Solomon says the plans of the heart belong to man, but the reply of the tongue is from the LORD. So the source of that reply is the LORD, not a person at the front of a room. Nice guess, friend, but the verse names Him plainly.

Yes, Solomon says exactly that. All a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are weighed out by the LORD (Proverbs 16:2). Everybody's own scale says they're doing great. I once stamped a cookie so crooked it looked like a map of a lake, and I still called it art.

Solomon actually says the opposite of what that statement denies. His motives are weighed out by the LORD (Proverbs 16:2). A man can think all his ways are pure in his own eyes, but the weighing belongs to the LORD. So the true answer is True.

explanations.answer: Commit your works to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one thing. Solomon says, "Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved." Hand the work over to Him and the promise comes with it. Short instruction, big promise, and no manual.

explanations.answer: Hide your plans from your enemies
explanations.explanation: Hiding plans is a common instinct, but Solomon doesn't say it here. The verse says, "Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved." The key is who you give the work to. Keeping it from your enemies isn't in the verse.

Hard work is good, but that's not the instruction in this verse. Solomon says, "Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved." The one thing is handing your works to the LORD. I've worked from morning to evening on a batch and still burned the bottoms, so effort alone isn't the promise.

Right, friend. Everyone who is proud in heart is detestable to the LORD, and Solomon says to be assured that he will not go unpunished (Proverbs 16:5). It's a serious line, so I'll just say it plainly. The proud heart doesn't get a pass.

explanations.answer: They will be given more time
explanations.explanation: More time isn't what the verse says. Solomon says the proud in heart are detestable to the LORD, and to be assured that he will not go unpunished (Proverbs 16:5). The verse doesn't offer an extension. It says the proud will not go unpunished.

explanations.answer: They will learn on their own
explanations.explanation: Learning on their own isn't in the verse. Solomon says everyone who is proud in heart is detestable to the LORD, and he adds, "be assured that he will not go unpunished." (Proverbs 16:5). I think the proud heart hopes it can figure everything out without help. Solomon doesn't say that, so I'll leave it there.

explanations.answer: By the fear of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Solomon says that by the fear of the LORD one turns aside from evil (Proverbs 16:6). Loving devotion and faithfulness are the first half, and the fear of the LORD is the second. Two halves, like a cookie snapped down the middle.

explanations.answer: By the counsel of the elders
explanations.explanation: Good counsel is helpful, but this verse doesn't name the elders. Solomon says that by the fear of the LORD one turns aside from evil (Proverbs 16:6). The fear of the LORD means honoring Him so much that you steer away from what He hates. That's how a person turns aside, according to this verse.

explanations.answer: By the strength of his hand
explanations.explanation: Strength of hand isn't in this verse. Solomon says that by the fear of the LORD one turns aside from evil (Proverbs 16:6). Turning aside from evil comes by the fear of the LORD, not by muscle. My mustache does all my lifting, and even it can't turn me from evil by force.

Yes! When a man's ways please the LORD, He makes even the man's enemies live at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). Even the enemies, friend. That's a promise bigger than any seating chart at a family cookout.

This one is actually true. Solomon says that when a man's ways please the LORD, He makes even the man's enemies live at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). The word "even" matters, because the enemies are included. So the right answer was True.

Yes, that's the one Solomon calls better. "Better a little with righteousness than great gain with injustice." The small pile with righteousness beats the big pile with injustice. I'll take a half-empty cookie box I earned honestly over a full one I shouldn't have.

That's the one Solomon puts second. He says, "Better a little with righteousness than great gain with injustice." The great gain sounds impressive, but the verse calls the little with righteousness better. Don't let a big pile fool you, friend.

Plenty with hard work isn't one of the options Solomon weighs. He says, "Better a little with righteousness than great gain with injustice." Notice what he puts on the scale: how a person got it, not just how much. The better one is the little with righteousness.

That's the word. A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps (Proverbs 16:9). The heart draws the map and the LORD determines the steps. I never planned on a cookie planet, friend, and yet here I am on a gold base with a mustache full of flour.

Wages are a fair guess, since money is on everybody's mind, but they aren't in this verse. Solomon says the LORD determines his steps (Proverbs 16:9). The heart plans a course, and the LORD determines the steps. That's the word that fits the blank.

Names matter to me, I had mine carved on my handle, but this verse doesn't say "name." Solomon says a man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps (Proverbs 16:9). The word that fits is steps. Plans and steps go together here.

Solomon says the opposite. Honest scales and balances are from the LORD, and all the weights in the bag are His concern (Proverbs 16:11). Every weight in that bag is His concern. So the statement is false.
Correct. Solomon says honest scales and balances are from the LORD, and "all the weights in the bag are His concern." Every weight in the bag is His concern. Honest weights matter to Him.
That's the word. Wicked behavior is detestable for kings, for a throne is established through righteousness (Proverbs 16:12). A throne stands on righteousness. It isn't built on a pile of cheating.

Conquest sounds like a king's business, but it's not what the verse says. Solomon says a throne is established through righteousness (Proverbs 16:12). Wicked behavior is detestable for kings. The throne stands on righteousness.

Wealth sounds like it would hold up a throne, but it's not the word here. Solomon says a throne is established through righteousness (Proverbs 16:12). Wicked behavior is detestable for kings, so righteousness is what holds the throne up. A big treasury isn't mentioned.

That's the word. The wrath of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it (Proverbs 16:14). The wise man calms it down. Walking into a room with an angry king and leaving calm takes real wisdom.

Riches aren't what Solomon names here. He says the wrath of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it (Proverbs 16:14). The one who pacifies it is the wise man. A fat wallet doesn't cool a king's temper in this verse.

Brave is a good quality, but it's not the word here. Solomon says a wise man will pacify the wrath of a king (Proverbs 16:14). Pacifying takes wisdom, not just courage. I'd be very brave for about two seconds and then hide behind the cooling rack.

Yes! When a king's face brightens, there is life, and his favor is like a rain cloud in spring (Proverbs 16:15). A spring rain cloud means good things are on the way. A king's favor is welcome like that.
A lamp in the night is a nice picture, but it isn't Solomon's. He says a king's favor is like a rain cloud in spring (Proverbs 16:15). The picture is rain, not light. Rain in spring is good news.

A tower isn't the picture here. Solomon says that when a king's face brightens, there is life, and his favor is like a rain cloud in spring (Proverbs 16:15). It's a cloud bringing rain, not a building. Favor that arrives like spring rain is a welcome thing.

Yes, "The highway of the upright leads away from evil…" Solomon adds that he who guards his way protects his life (Proverbs 16:17). The upright keep traveling away from evil. That's a highway worth staying on.
Riches are not where Solomon says this highway goes. He says the highway of the upright leads away from evil (Proverbs 16:17). Its direction is away from evil. Guarding your way protects your life.

Kings do show up in this chapter, so I see why you picked the court. But Solomon says the highway of the upright leads away from evil (Proverbs 16:17). That's where it heads. The king's court isn't mentioned in this verse.

That's the word. Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). Pride walks in first and a fall follows. I once strutted across my bakery like I owned the place and slid face-first into the chocolate chips.
A reward sounds nice, but it's not what follows pride here. Solomon says a haughty spirit goes before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). The word is fall. Pride goes first and the fall comes after.

A promotion would be a lovely thing to follow a haughty spirit, but the verse says otherwise. Solomon says pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). The word is fall. I'm sorry to tell you, friend, the proverb is not a career guide.

Solomon says the reverse. "It is better to be lowly in spirit among the humble than to divide the spoil with the proud." (Proverbs 16:19). Splitting the loot with proud company isn't the better deal. So the statement is false.

Correct. Solomon says, "It is better to be lowly in spirit among the humble than to divide the spoil with the proud." Being lowly among the humble beats a share of the spoil with the proud. A smaller seat with good company is the better one.

explanations.answer: He who trusts in the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes. Whoever heeds instruction will find success, "…and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD." The blessed one is the one who trusts. Trust is the word to hold onto here.

Working hard is good, but Solomon doesn't call that person blessed here. He says whoever heeds instruction will find success, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD (Proverbs 16:20). The blessing goes to trust in the LORD. Effort isn't the measure in this verse.

Friends are a gift, but this verse doesn't count them. Solomon says whoever heeds instruction will find success, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD (Proverbs 16:20). The blessed one is the one who trusts in the LORD. A big contact list doesn't make the list.

That's the word. Understanding is a fountain of life to its possessor, but the discipline of fools is folly (Proverbs 16:22). A fountain of life on one side and folly on the other. Solomon sets the two side by side so you can see the difference.

Wisdom is the opposite of what the verse says. Solomon says understanding is a fountain of life to its possessor, but the discipline of fools is folly (Proverbs 16:22). The fool's discipline ends up as folly. Wisdom belongs with the first half.

Strength isn't what the verse gives the fool. Solomon says the discipline of fools is folly (Proverbs 16:22). I think that means a fool can work hard at correcting himself and still end up in the same foolish place. Understanding is the one that is a fountain of life to its possessor.
Yes. Solomon says, "The heart of the wise man instructs his mouth and adds persuasiveness to his lips." (Proverbs 16:23). The heart teaches the mouth what to say. That's a mouth with good training.

That one is actually true. Solomon says the heart of the wise man instructs his mouth and adds persuasiveness to his lips (Proverbs 16:23). The heart does the instructing, and persuasiveness comes with it. So the right answer was True.

Yes! "Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones." Solomon says a kind word does good for the whole person, soul and bones (Proverbs 16:24). Sweet to the soul and healing to the bones is a lot for a few words to do. Pleasant words are worth handing out.
A fresh spring is a nice picture, but it's not Solomon's. He says pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones (Proverbs 16:24). Sweet is the clue. A honeycomb fits it.

A morning mist isn't the picture here. Solomon says pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones (Proverbs 16:24). The word sweet points right to it. Gentle words do real good.
That's the word, and it's a heavy one. "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." (Proverbs 16:25). The way only seems right. Its end is the way of death.

Life would be a happy ending, but the verse says otherwise. Solomon says there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death (Proverbs 16:25). It's a heavy line, so I'll say it plainly. The way only seems right, and the end is death.

Peace would be a nice place for a road to end, but that's not what Solomon says. He says there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death (Proverbs 16:25). It's a heavy verse. The word that fits is death.
Yes. Solomon says a worker's appetite works for him because his hunger drives him onward (Proverbs 16:26). The hunger does some of the pushing. It's why the oven opens early at my place.
Actually, that's true. Solomon says a worker's appetite works for him because his hunger drives him onward (Proverbs 16:26). The hunger itself keeps him moving. So the right answer was True.

That's what Solomon says. "A perverse man spreads dissension, and a gossip divides close friends." (Proverbs 16:28). Close friends are the ones who get split. Gossip is a small thing that does big damage.

That's the opposite of what Solomon says. He says a gossip divides close friends (Proverbs 16:28). Instead of bringing people together, gossip splits up the ones who were close. It's a mess to clean up.

A gossip keeping secrets safe would be a very short job description, and that's not the verse. Solomon says a gossip divides close friends (Proverbs 16:28). Gossip splits up friends. That's the damage he names.

explanations.answer: Down a path that is not good
explanations.explanation: Yes. A violent man entices his neighbor and leads him down a path that is not good (Proverbs 16:29). He doesn't stay on the path alone. He takes his neighbor with him.

explanations.answer: Into the house of the king
explanations.explanation: The king has been in this chapter a lot, but he isn't in this verse. Solomon says a violent man entices his neighbor and leads him down a path that is not good (Proverbs 16:29). The neighbor ends up on a path that is not good. The king's house isn't the destination.

explanations.answer: Out to the edge of town
explanations.explanation: The edge of town isn't named here. Solomon says a violent man entices his neighbor and leads him down a path that is not good (Proverbs 16:29). The path is described by what it is, not where it is. It's one that is not good.

Yes. Gray hair is a crown of glory, and Solomon says it is attained along the path of righteousness (Proverbs 16:31). It's a glad line in a chapter with some heavy ones. The crown comes along that path.
That one is true. Solomon says gray hair is a crown of glory, and it is attained along the path of righteousness (Proverbs 16:31). The crown comes along that path. So the right answer was True.

That's the word. "He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city." (Proverbs 16:32). Controlling your temper is called greater than capturing a city. It's harder than it sounds, especially when the oven door slams on your mustache.

A scholar is a nice comparison, but it's not Solomon's. He says he who is slow to anger is better than a warrior (Proverbs 16:32). He also says controlling your temper is greater than capturing a city. The word that fits the blank is warrior.

A merchant isn't in this verse. Solomon says he who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city (Proverbs 16:32). One line names a warrior and the other names someone who captures a city. The word for the blank is warrior.

Yes. "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." It looks like chance, but Solomon says every decision of the lot is from Him. A lot was a way of making a choice by casting it. So the answer is the LORD.

The one who casts the lot seems like the obvious pick, but Solomon says otherwise. "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." The person throws it, but the decision comes from the LORD. It's a good thing to remember the next time something looks like luck.

The king has been busy in this chapter, but he doesn't decide this one. Solomon says, "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." Every decision of the lot is from the LORD, not the king. Even a king doesn't get this call.
